meta.title: Headless API
meta.description: The same model without the markup: the hooks and the controller behind the components.

demos.headless: A schedule with markup of your own

basics.intro: When slots and render props are not enough — a different structure, not a different look — take the model and leave the markup. useScheduler returns everything <Scheduler> renders from: the shifts with their items, the pinned set, the navigation state, the formatters, and a getter for each element’s props.
points: Spread getRootProps, getScrollerProps and getSectionProps and the measurements work: compact mode, the active shift, the navigation.
Spread getItemProps on whatever you make a card, and activation, the keyboard and focus work as they do in the built-in one.
getPinSentinelProps is what makes pinning work in your markup; without it, items never pin.
The state is the same one the components use, so nothing is missing and nothing is duplicated.

layers.intro: The package is three layers, and you can enter at any of them:
points: @react-schedulerkit/react-scheduler — the components, the hooks and the types.
/core — the pure functions behind them: shifts, bucketing, the timeline layout, the formatters. No React, no DOM; it runs in plain Node, and that is tested.
/dom — the browser engines: the pin observer, the navigator, the width and motion observers. DOM, no React.
/headless — createScheduler, the framework-agnostic controller with the state, the actions and a subscription.
The getters carry the roles, the names and the keyboard handling. Spread them and the accessibility comes with them; leave them out and it is yours to build.
The live region, the announcements and the focus return are part of the components, not of the hook: a headless rendering provides its own.
The order you render the sections and the cards in is the order a screen reader reads, so keep it the order of the day.
useScheduler for a React rendering of your own; createScheduler for another framework entirely.
useShiftModel, useTimelineLayout, usePinOnPass, useShiftNavigation, useNow and useCompact are the pieces, if you want only one of them.
The pure functions of /core are useful on a server: bucketing items or computing a layout needs no browser.
The stylesheet is written for the built-in markup. A headless rendering brings its own CSS, or uses base.css as a starting point.
The overflow dialog and the detail dialog are components, not state: a headless rendering opens its own.
The hook returns a new state object on every relevant change; memoize what you build from it if your rendering is expensive.
